newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-CWS steps up action against stalker.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CWS steps up action against stalker.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) on Wednesday stepped up its offensive against a predator that has been stalking it for months, gaining a court order that led to the return of confidential papers.
The society's move against a 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) takeover bid resulted in the return of seven boxes of the documents.

CWS said it was obvious the papers returned by entrepreneur Andrew Regan and others involved in the bid plans were CWS property. It has written to the parties concerned asking which documents had been shown to advisors and whether anyone had asked where they came from or how they were obtained.

"The affidavits filed at court by Andrew Regan and his fellow conspirators tell an extraordinary story," the CWS said, adding that CWS manager Allan Green, who was suspended last week, had been passing on documents over many months "and it appears he was encouraged to do that by Mr.Regan and David Lyons".

Lyons is a close business associate of Regan and a former CWS advisor. Lyons, Regan and merchant bank Hambros, which was asked by CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth how much it knew about the origin of the internal minutes and board papers, were not immediately available for comment.

Earlier, Galileo made a plea to end the legal actions which have thwarted its plans but this was later rejected by CWS chairman Lennox Fyfe who said CWS intends pressing on with legal proceedings and "to secure a judgement for substantial damages" against Lyons and others involved in the bid.
Galileo, set up to bid for the 153-year-old mutually owned supermarkets-to-funeral parlour group by Regan, also said the information had been given to it voluntarily by a member of the CWS staff.
It said it was not seeking court permission to publish its bid proposal. The court is expected to rule on what it can use on Friday although CWS said it was seeking to make the injunction permanent.

Galileo's plan to bid for the CWS was temporarily stopped in its tracks by the group's unexpected legal move. This resulted from information uncovered by the CWS through a firm of private investigators.
Last Thursday, CWS suspended two of its senior managers for alleged serious breach of trust after its video surveillance revealed that one of the men had met Regan and an associate.
Galileo, an offshoot of 31-year-old Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, said it was making a direct plea to each CWS director to explain its position.

It said it was inviting the CWS board "to consider whether, in preference to continued legal proceedings, it would be in the best interests of members to receive details of the proposal and allow them to reach a decision".

But CWS chairman Fyfe said he had instructed CWS directors to return the proposal "unopened and unread". Galileo has not revealed any details of its ambitious plan to break open the labyrinthine structure of the Co-op but has said it would propose a special meeting to convert the group into a limited company which it would then buy.
On Tuesday it emerged that Galileo had arranged a 1.2 billion pound debt facility with Japanese securities giant Nomura. Galileo is known to be backed by a number of City institutions.
Nomura declined to detail this arrangement, but banking sources said the plans had been put together by the firm's innovative principal finance group.
This has been behind a number of high-profile but controversial deals, including a rail rolling stock privatisation and the sale of British Ministry of Defence housing.

Manchester-based CWS owns the profitable Co-operative Bank as well as large British insurer Co-operative Insurance Society (CIS). It is also one of the country's largest undertakers and has other interests ranging from farms to opticians.

The Co-op Bank is seen as the jewel in the CWS crown, with pre-tax profits last year of 45.5 million pounds, but on Wednesday its chairman Alan Prescott told a meeting of the bank's managers that it was not for sale, repeating a now familiar message. Regan has been portrayed as an asset-stripper by the Co-op and it is widely accepted that if the Galileo bid were to succeed, parts of the CWS would be sold off, with potential buyers such as Allied Irish Banks already in the frame to buy the Co-op Bank.
